rationale: The anxiety discussion concerns Crocus extracts or components. There is no cold-pressed sesame oil intervention or anxiety assessment.
The investigator overview links a Parkinson sage cognition pilot and a separate Alzheimer's sage trial. Sleep examples concern other plants. It provides no dried-sage insomnia comparison.
The saffron table concerns dementia cognition. Depression examples for behavioral symptoms involve other botanicals. No ground-saffron depressive symptom comparison is given.
The depression section cites saffron preparations in non-Parkinson depression, including active comparators. It does not isolate ground saffron in Parkinson disease.

The review cites saffron extracts and crocin add-on trials in major depression. Its Alzheimer clinical studies measured cognition and function. It reports no separate Parkinson powder–depression result.
Safranal was used in conditioning neural cells before transplantation. Results address graft survival, dopamine markers and drug-elicited rotations. Depression was not measured.

The Crocus depression citation is an imipramine comparison in major depression. The other cited papers use experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. They supply no clinical Parkinson depression estimate.

Table 3 has an inconclusive depression interaction (p=.467) in adults with poor sleep and normal baseline mood scores. The trial assigned standardized extract and explicitly excluded Parkinson disease.
Central crocin was tested in sleep-deprived rats using a hot-plate endpoint. There is no separate depressive symptom assessment or oral ground-saffron arm.
The depression section discusses isolated crocetin and restraint-stress swimming and biomarkers in rodents. It is a separate preparation and endpoint from a human Parkinson depression measure.
The clinical mood section lists saffron extracts and petal or stigma comparisons in patients with major depression. No separately measured ground-saffron Parkinson depression comparison is supplied.
The depression table mixes rodent activity outcomes and ethanol-extract papers in clinical depression. None measures the named ground preparation for Parkinson depression.
The isolated compounds were tested against acrylamide neurotoxicity. The behavioral result is gait and the other outcomes are oxidative or cellular. Depression was not measured.
No fresh rosemary was assigned. The study tests crocetin and an amide under acrylamide exposure and does not measure depressive symptoms.
The pain examples use Crocus or traditional mixtures, with no comparison isolating toasted sesame oil.
Saffron appears in an Alzheimer's cognition comparison. The sleep sections describe lemon balm with valerian and other mixtures. They give no saffron insomnia result.
The use table lists valerian and kava under sleep problems. Saffron's sedative characterization supplies no dedicated insomnia-severity measure.
Sleep deprivation defines the model. The reported dependent variable is thermal withdrawal latency after central crocin, so the result supplies no insomnia severity direction.
The sleep section points to Gardenia-derived crocetin and a separate isolated-crocetin EEG trial. The original trial outcomes and botanical origin differ from oral culinary saffron insomnia severity.

The review retells a traditional use of saffron water for insomnia. Its earlier reference specifies an external preparation. Neither source observes an oral ground-stigma effect in Parkinson patients.
The overview reports global sleep quality and separately summarizes insomnia adverse events. It does not isolate insomnia severity in Parkinson disease or characterize culinary ground stigma.
Clinical depression examples compare Crocus formulations. No cold-pressed sesame oil exposure or attributable depression score appears.
Olive oil is mentioned as part of a topical gynecological mixture. The anxiety evidence does not test cold-pressed olive oil.
The turmeric section concerns curcumin, immune signaling and autoimmune disease model severity. It gives no grated-turmeric estimate for muscle rigidity.
The review's turmeric and curcumin studies cover strength and locomotor tasks. Its separate explicit rigidity score belongs to the Nigella section. No grated-turmeric rigidity comparison appears.

Figures 2–3 report rotations and transplanted-cell outcomes after exposure to safranal-treated cells in a Parkinson-like model. The comparison gives no passive-rigidity measure or ground-stigma effect.
The saffron references address mood and neuroinflammation in another setting. There is no measurement of separately assessed rigidity after ground saffron.
The mouse study used isolated oral crocetin. Figure 1 reports rotarod, hanging and pole performance. Passive rigidity and culinary saffron are outside the measured comparison.
Saffron and crocin studies measure dopaminergic markers or hanging performance. The explicit rigidity model belongs to Nigella. The cultural smooth-muscle note provides no clinical rigidity measure.

Ground stigma was used in composition analysis. Purified crocin I produced favorable pole and open-field outcomes in the separate mouse experiment. Molecular complex rigidity is unrelated to muscle rigidity.
The saffron table cites an Alzheimer's donepezil comparison with global cognition outcomes. It provides no isolated executive function measure with dried saffron in Parkinson disease.
The fatigue citation involves the isolated compound crocetin and exercise performance in healthy adults. It is a different exposure and endpoint from dried-saffron Parkinson fatigue.
The Parkinson sections review experimental neuroprotection and model observations. No clinical fatigue severity contrast with dried saffron appears.
The fatigue references in the use table concern ginkgo and ginseng. The saffron section provides no clinical fatigue comparison.
The sleep studies' sleepiness and morning refreshment measures do not provide a Parkinson fatigue-severity contrast. No dried-stigma fatigue comparison appears.
The fatigue mention points to a prior pooled mood review across preparations and populations. There is no independent dried-saffron Parkinson fatigue estimate.
The cardiovascular table uses fatigue to describe rabbit atrioventricular-node physiology. It supplies no symptom fatigue or oral dried-saffron comparison.
Gait score and cortical oxidative markers supply no fatigue-severity endpoint or dried culinary saffron arm.
The pain model tests isolated crocetin after nerve injury and does not assign or measure dried date fruit.
Crocus traditional pain preparations and molecule studies do not assign Phoenix dactylifera fruit or measure its effect on pain.
Its symptom and safety tables concern saffron interventions. No dried-date fruit exposure or fruit-specific pain outcome appears.
The ginger section reviews shogaols and immunological markers in laboratory or autoimmune models. No rigidity estimate is given for consumed grated ginger.
The cranberry section concerns juice or capsule preparations in urinary infection and bacterial adhesion. No dried cranberry depression comparison appears.
In the ginger section gingerols and shogaols are linked to neuroinflammatory markers. The cited results do not separately assess pain severity after grated ginger in Parkinson disease.
The behavioral section discusses ginkgo and other named botanical interventions. There is no dried Phoenix dactylifera fruit intervention or date-associated apathy estimate.
Turmeric is listed as a potential adulterant of ground saffron in the authentication section. It is not a studied turmeric preparation for pain.
The turmeric section concerns inflammation and experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, not a culinary ground turmeric pain comparison.
The grape section discusses resveratrol chemistry and experimental signaling. It does not assign or measure raw grape for anxiety.
Grape-derived phenolics and neuroprotective mechanisms are distinct from a frozen-grape exposure. No attributable rigidity outcome appears.
The insomnia tradition involves saffron water. Olive oil appears in a separate topical gynecological mixture, without an extra-virgin olive oil insomnia comparison.
The sage section identifies the small Parkinson cognition pilot. In this overview the apathy analysis is for ginkgo. Neither the pilot summary nor its later grant account provides a sage apathy item.
Ginger is proposed for gastrointestinal tolerability of dementia drugs. There is no grated-ginger anxiety comparison. The review's anxiety discussion treats other herbs.
The anxiety sections concern herbs other than ginger. Ginger extract and constituent work covers inflammation without a measured grated-ginger anxiety result.
The green tea section concerns tea extracts or catechins and inflammation. Fatigue comparisons in the use table are for other botanicals. No brewed-tea fatigue outcome is given.
Hot-plate withdrawal latency is the experimental outcome. The deprivation equipment is not a measure of fall frequency, and the study has no oral ground-saffron arm.
The longer rotarod latency under crocetin is a motor coordination result in a provoked task. It does not establish a count of spontaneous or recurrent falls after ground saffron.
